question_text: Across the verses, what does the pattern of engagement and non-engagement with perception indicate about the characteristic's nature?

distinct_answers.text: [Sub-group not separately addressed in source — see cluster-level finding (cluster_subgroup_id IS NULL) for this prompt]

M06 characteristics are perception-organising phenomena. Each characteristic establishes a framework through which subsequent perceptions are filtered and interpreted. Rightly-directed characteristics (righteous hatred, righteous abhorrence) sharpen and clarify perception of moral reality. Disordered characteristics (person-directed hatred, contempt, inverted abhorrence, cruelty, malice) impair, bypass, or invert the accurate perception of persons, worth, and moral reality. The cluster as a whole reveals that how the inner being is oriented fundamentally shapes what and how the person perceives.

---

### T3.2 — Cognition
[Sub-group not separately addressed in source — see cluster-level finding for this prompt]

Perception is the primary trigger for M05-B (compassion) and M05-F (comfort) — both are activated by the perceptive encounter with another's suffering. The other sub-groups engage perception more peripherally. This cluster-level pattern confirms that the cluster's characteristics are constitutively relational — they are not self-generated in isolation but activated by the encounter with another person's inner reality (suffering, need, invitation to fellowship). The characteristics require the perceptive faculty to be activated, even when perception is not the primary or ongoing constitutional engagement.

**[CLUSTER]** E. The consistent enabling of perception by righteousness and impairing by wickedness reveals that righteousness is not morally neutral in its cognitive effects — it is epistemologically transforming. The righteous person perceives what the wicked cannot. This is a significant finding for the programme: righteousness is not only a moral condition but a perceptual condition. The inner state of righteousness enables a kind of seeing; its absence produces a kind of blindness.

Governance perception (VCG03 Solomon's governance discernment), directional perception (VCG04 things of God vs flesh), intelligibility perception (VCG08 understanding Scripture). Wisdom's perceptive range is oriented and directional — it perceives in relation to God and right action.
Range: understanding God's ways, prophecy, teaching, strategic situations. The range is broad but coherent: understanding is always the act of grasping the meaning-structure of something.
Widest perceptive range in M15: material (VCG10), relational (VCG04, VCG11), moral (VCG07), propositional (VCG08), divine-comprehensive (VCG01).
Range: prudent-action perception (VCG01), self-evaluative perception (VCG02), gustatory-testing perception (VCG05). All directed at discriminating distinctions.
Perceptive range is secondary: observation feeds foresight (VCG08 ant). Other VCGs focus on the volitional-deliberative act.
Range: inward (VCG04 Daniel's vision), retrospective (VCG02 Joseph), receptive (VCG03 God's law). All directed at received content.
Perceptive range does not apply to M15-G as content-holder.
Range is differentiated by the inner condition of the perceiver: the same logos perceived as folly or power (VCG01).
Perceptive range not applicable.
Anxiety impairs perception by filling the inner person with preoccupying concerns that crowd out alertness to God's action and to eschatological realities.

Doubt engages the perceptive faculty but cannot complete the process — the person is stuck between seeing and trusting.

---

### T3.2 — Cognition

Grace opens access: the verse evidence consistently shows that received grace enables a perceptive encounter with God (face-seeing in Job 33:26) that was not previously available. The hearing/grace pairing (984-001) reveals that grace is sought precisely because the person recognises their perceptive access to God depends on divine response. Grace is the condition of sustained divine-human perceptive contact.

Goodness produces accurate perception: the good person sees correctly (Jer 1:12). The characteristic is not only a moral quality but an epistemological one — goodness shapes the accuracy of inner sight.

---

### T3.2 — Cognition

The wealth domain systematically engages the perceptive faculty — but primarily to impair or distort it (M46-A: closed; M46-B: never satisfied / deceived) or to redirect it (M46-D: toward the true wealth). The perception of wealth is almost never a neutral perceptual act in Scripture's account. This confirms the domain-cluster character of M46: wealth is never a neutral object of perception; it always either impairs perception of God's reality (M46-A, M46-B) or requires the deliberate redirecting of perception (M46-D).

The pattern reveals that fear is a perceptively-saturated characteristic: it is triggered by perception (sight, hearing) and it modifies perception (enabling or impairing). Ordered fear (M01-A) enables a clearer perception of God and reality; disordered fear (M01-D's dismay, M01-B's social fear) systematically distorts or shuts down perception. This is a significant finding: the presence or absence of correctly ordered fear shapes what the person can see and hear accurately. The cluster confirms that fear is not merely an inner experience but a perceptual orientation — it determines what the person is able to register about the world.

**Contrast: D-VCG-03 vs B-VCG-03:** The pattern reveals a fundamental asymmetry: morally-calibrated anger is triggered by accurate moral perception (Act 17:16; Neh 5:6) and enhances the moral clarity of the person who experiences it. Ungoverned/possessing anger bypasses perception and drives action from its own momentum (Est 3:5; Dan 3:13). The characteristic's relationship to perception is the primary marker of whether the anger is rightly ordered or disordered.

Grief is a perception-responsive characteristic: it arises when the inner person perceives something that matters being lost, harmed, or violated. The perceptive faculty is the trigger that activates grief — the person must perceive the loss or the sin before grief can arise. This means grief is not arbitrary or groundless; it is the appropriate inner-being response to perceived reality. The characteristic's perception-dependence also means that those whose perceptive faculty is dulled (by pride, self-deception, or moral hardening) will not grieve when grief is appropriate — confirming the T1.7.2 finding about inner conditions blocking reception.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Exultation is a perceptually-grounded characteristic — it is not emotionally autonomous but arises from and depends upon the accurate perception of who God is and what he has done. Where perception is accurate (God's salvation seen and received), exultation follows. Where perception is distorted (idol-worship, Hos 10:5; spiritual prostitution, Hos 9:1), exultation misfires toward wrong objects.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Joy is a perceptually-grounded characteristic whose depth depends on the depth of perception that grounds it. Surface-level perception → surface-level joy (rocky-ground hearer); accurate, deep perception of divine reality → sustained, transforming joy (Hab 3:18 type; Psa 97:8). The pattern reveals that the quality of a person's inner perception of who God is and what he has done is the single most important determinant of the quality and durability of their Joy.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Suffering-Joy is the characteristic most directly associated with faith-perception — the inner-being capacity to perceive what is not yet visible. Its connection with the Spirit (who enables perception of divine realities) and its consistent grounding in eschatological realities (heaven's reward, Christ's glory) confirm it as the characteristic that most fully engages the perceptive faculty in its spiritual-discernment mode rather than its sensory mode.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Gladness is perception-dependent in a way that distinguishes it from Joy (which can be commanded even when circumstances are adverse) — Gladness requires the accurate perception of genuine goodness before it can arise. The pattern reveals that forming the perceptive-evaluative faculty is essential to Gladness's health: moral formation that trains perception trains Gladness.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Delight functions as a perceptive lens: it shapes what the person attends to, dwells in, and is drawn toward. Delight in God's word produces sustained perceptive engagement with Scripture; Delight in the wrong object (beast, idols, abominations) produces captivated perceptive fixation on the wrong thing. The pattern reveals that Delight and perception are mutually shaping: Delight directs the perceptive faculty toward its object, and continued perception reinforces and deepens the Delight. This makes the formation of right Delight a perceptive-shaping act.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Pleasure is uniquely perception-dependent among M04 characteristics — it arises from sensory encounter with what is genuinely pleasant. The pattern reveals that training perception rightly is essential to genuine Pleasure: the person whose perceptive faculty is attuned to genuine goodness receives genuine Pleasure; the person whose perception is distorted (by folly, false objects, covenant-unfaithfulness) receives counterfeit Pleasure that cannot sustain or nourish.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Wonder is the characteristic most directly dependent on and productive of genuine perception. It requires the person to genuinely see what is happening (Psa 107:24 — "they saw the deeds of the Lord") and it deepens the person's capacity to see (Psa 119:18 — open my eyes to behold). The pattern reveals perception-training as essential to Wonder-formation: communities that regularly tell of God's wondrous works (VCG-01 proclamatory tradition) are training the perceptive capacity of their members to see God's acts as extraordinary.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster as a whole is perceptually grounded — all seven characteristics arise from or depend upon genuine perception of what is real. The pattern reveals that the quality of a person's inner perceptive engagement with reality determines the quality of their positive inner-being states. This is the cluster's first-order formative principle: train perception rightly and the positive characteristics follow; distort perception and the characteristics are distorted or misdirected. The Wonder (Char 6) corpus makes this most explicit through its Tell-Remember-Meditate pattern: the community that regularly rehearses God's wondrous acts is training its perceptive capacity to see God's acts as extraordinary. The implication extends to the whole cluster: liturgical and worship practices that repeatedly engage perception with God's acts, character, and promises are the primary formation mechanisms for the cluster's positive inner states.

**[CHAR-1]** E — That shame operates bidirectionally on perception: in its destructive form (unjust wound, moral paralysis) it closes perception down; in its constructive form (corrective shame before God's holiness) it opens perception to what was previously obscured. This bidirectional relation confirms that the quality of shame's perceptive effect depends on whether the person's will is engaged constructively (receiving the corrective signal) or not (paralysed by the wound or hardened against correction).

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 primarily impairs perception by collapsing the upward gaze: the humiliated are "dismayed and confounded." The haughty eyes targeted in Isa 5:15 and Psa 18:27 show the perceptive faculty as the site of prideful distortion. In the VCG-03 divine-abasement mode, CHAR-2 can be read as perception-correcting: the proud are forced to see what they actually are.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 is produced by failed perception — the judge who does not see the worth of persons (Luk 18:2/4); dishonoring God through hypocrisy while not perceiving the self-contradiction (Rom 2:23). CHAR-3 impairs the relational-perceptive faculty in the dishonorer.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 engages moral perception — the conscience that recognises "certain deeds done in secret are so morally degraded that even speaking of them is shameful" (Eph 5:12) is exercising moral-perceptive discernment. The inverted conscience (VCG-03) shows distorted moral perception: what should be seen as shameful is seen as honourable.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — Perception is engaged in CHAR-5 through the contempt-er's misperception of worth (they do not see the genuine worth of the person they despise) and through the recipient's perception of their own contempt-received condition. Psa 14:6 — "shame the plans of the poor" — shows how contempt targets the poor person's inner plans and confidence (their hopeful perception of their own possibilities). CHAR-5 impairs the recipient's hopeful perception by forcing them to see themselves through the contempt-er's false worth-assessment.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 enables moral perception: the person with a clean conscience and blameless hands can perceive their own moral condition accurately (they know they are innocent) and can perceive God's response accurately (God confirms the innocent's claim, Gen 20:6). The loss of CHAR-6 impairs moral perception: Psa 73:13's crisis is a perceptive failure — the psalmist cannot perceive why innocent suffering exists; Hos 8:5's incapacity-for-innocence is a state in which the people cannot perceive their own moral condition accurately because it has been so long distorted by idolatry.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's perceptual engagement reveals a consistent bidirectional pattern: shame impairs horizontal perception (the humiliated cannot see their situation clearly; the contempt-shamed person cannot see their own worth accurately) while corrective shame can deepen vertical perception (Char 1 M07-C — shame before God enabling the person to see what God requires; Char 5 — divine reversal correcting the world's perceptual distortions). Every form of shame involves a distorted perception that needs correction. Haughty eyes (Char 2 — Isa 5:15; Psa 18:27) are the perceptive faculty's pride-distorted form; the seared conscience (Chars 1, 4) is the perceptive faculty's moral-distorted form; contempt (Char 5) is the perceptive faculty's worth-distorted form. The cluster's positive pole (Char 6) represents the perceptive faculty in its undistorted form — seeing one's moral condition accurately enough to claim innocence before God.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The consistent pattern of perceptive impairment reveals that CHAR-1 is a self-sealing characteristic: it closes off the very perceptual capacities that would detect and correct it. The proud person does not see God's standards (Psa 10:5, vc=34166), does not see divine majesty (Isa 26:10, vc=34024), does not seek God (Psa 10:4, vc=34074), and — as will emerge in T3.3 — does not perceive the redemptive history that would generate gratitude (Deu 8:14, vc=34223; Hos 13:6, vc=34232). The perceptive closure means CHAR-1 removes the inputs through which correction could enter. This is why the wisdom corpus (Pro 16:18, vc=34073, M08-A1-VCG-03: "pride goes before destruction") names external catastrophe rather than internal perception as the corrective mechanism — the perceptive faculty that would otherwise generate self-correction has been closed.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The pattern reveals that CHAR-2, like CHAR-1, is partially self-sealing: it closes the perceptive faculty for divine authority that would check the will's transgression. Psa 86:14 (vc=34097): "they do not set God before them" — removing the perception of God prevents the inner corrective response that God's perceived authority would generate. However, CHAR-2's perceptive impairment is specifically targeted at authority figures (God, "glorious ones," appointed judges) rather than the broader perceptive closure evidenced in CHAR-1.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The pattern reveals that CHAR-3 selectively impairs the perceptive faculty in the direction of self-inconsistency: the boaster can perceive their achievement but cannot perceive the gap between their self-presentation and their actual state. This is the perceptive analogue of 1Cor 4:7 (vc=33871)'s cognitive misattribution: the boaster misperceives the origin of their goods AND cannot perceive the discrepancy between the boast and reality.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The pattern confirms CHAR-4 as self-sealing at the cognitive level: the inflated self-picture closes the perceptive faculty that would correct it. 1Ti 6:4 (vc=33925): the conceited person "understands nothing" — the comprehensive epistemic failure means there is no internal perceptive basis for correction. This is the most extreme form of perceptive self-sealing in M08: where CHAR-1 closes perception of God, CHAR-4 closes perception of reality in general (understanding nothing), making it particularly resistant to evidence-based correction.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The pattern confirms CHAR-5 as self-sealing at the perceptive level in the structural register: the structural power that generates CHAR-5 simultaneously becomes the perceptive barrier that prevents the person from seeing their actual vulnerability. Obd 3 (vc=65674): "the pride of your heart has deceived you" — the deception is perceptual. This makes CHAR-5's reversal particularly sudden from the human perspective: the proud-might nation cannot see the judgment coming until the structural power that was its perceptive barrier is removed.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster-level perceptive pattern reveals the theological structure of pride: pride systematically closes the inner eyes that would show the person their actual position before God. The pattern is not accidental — it is intrinsic to what pride is. M08 characteristics impair perception not randomly but precisely at the perceptions that would dissolve them: if you could see God clearly (CHAR-1's closure), you would not elevate yourself above your proper station; if you could see your self-inconsistency clearly (CHAR-3's closure), you would not boast in the law while breaking it; if you could see your actual vulnerability (CHAR-5's closure), you would not declare "I am, and there is no one besides me." The cluster-synthesis: M08 is the cluster of the closed inner eye.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The auditory-perceptive pattern reveals that submission is constitutively *responsive*: it cannot originate from the person alone but requires something heard — a word, a command, a gospel claim — to which the will yields. This confirms that submission is a *relational-responsive* characteristic rather than a self-generated one: it is the inner side of the person's response to a genuine address from a legitimate authority. The hupakoē root makes this permanent: submission is, at its root, "hearing-under" — the will that receives and yields rather than deflects or resists.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that contrition is constitutively epistemic at its ground: it requires genuine inner seeing of what is true about oneself before God. The person who is genuinely contrite is one who has seen accurately — their spirit crushed by what genuine moral self-knowledge before divine holiness reveals. This makes contrition a characteristic that cannot be faked at the perceptive level: genuine crushing requires genuine perception of the reality that occasions it.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The pattern reveals that metriopatheō (Heb5:2) depends on a double perceptive act: (a) accurate perception of one's own creaturely limitation; and (b) accurate perception of the other's wayward condition through the lens of that shared limitation. The characteristic thus deepens perception by requiring it to be both self-directed and other-directed simultaneously — the gentle person is one who genuinely sees both themselves and others with the same accuracy that shared human experience enables.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The pattern reveals that semnotēs operates partly through others' perception of the person's settled gravity — it is not merely an inner state but one that produces a perceptual field around the person in which genuine authority and authenticity can be received. The characteristic thus has an outward-perceptual dimension: it shapes how others receive the person's presence, instruction, and authority by providing a clear, undistorted signal of settled moral gravity.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The pattern reveals that willing-heartedness determines whether the call to free giving is received as invitation or experienced as burden. The willing-hearted person (Exo35:5/22) perceives the call as an opportunity for free expression; the person whose spirit is not yet willing (Psa51:12 — pre-restoration) perceives the same call as an obligation they cannot freely fulfil. The characteristic thus shapes the perceptive faculty's reception of calls to giving and service.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The pattern reveals that humility is constitutively *receptive*: the characteristic is the inner posture that allows genuine perception because it does not interpose the self's self-protective distortions between the person and what is genuinely real. The proud person (Zedekiah in 2Ch36:12; the Col2:18 person) cannot genuinely hear because their self-enclosure filters incoming reality through the lens of self-preservation. The humble person (Josiah in 2Ch34:27; Paul in Act20:19) is genuinely open to being addressed, corrected, and informed. Humility is thus not merely one characteristic among others but a structural enabler of perceptive functioning — the inner condition without which the person cannot genuinely hear God or others.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster-wide perceptive engagement pattern reveals that M09 characteristics are constitutively receptive — they are inner postures that allow genuine perception precisely because they do not interpose self-protective distortions between the person and what is genuinely real. The most diagnostic contrast is between CHAR-1 Humility and its structural opposite: the proud person (Zedekiah in 2Ch36:12; the Col2:18 person) cannot genuinely hear because self-enclosure filters reality; the humble person (Josiah in 2Ch34:27) is genuinely open to being addressed. Submission (CHAR-2) is the characteristic most constitutively shaped by the perceptive faculty — hupakoē's root (under-hearing) encodes reception of spoken authority as its constitutional origin. Contrition (CHAR-3) reveals perception as its epistemic precondition: the person who is genuinely contrite has seen accurately — their spirit crushed by genuine moral self-knowledge before divine holiness. Meekness and Gentleness (CHAR-4) deepens perception by requiring it in two directions simultaneously: genuine self-perception (of one's own weakness) and accurate other-perception (of the erring person's condition). Dignity (CHAR-5) operates partly through the perceptual field created in others — the dignified person is perceived as genuinely authoritative without self-promotion. Willing-heartedness (CHAR-6) determines whether the call to give is received as invitation or burden. Cluster-level: M09 is a perception-enabling cluster — every characteristic functions to remove the perceptive distortions that self-assertion produces.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The pattern reveals that wilful sinning is in part a *perceptive failure* — the will commits the known wrong when the inner perception of God's holiness and the moral gravity of the act fails to register with sufficient force to deter. Joseph's refusal (Gen 39:9) operates because his perception is active and named ("great wickedness, sin against God"). The deterrence corpus (VCG-03: Exo 20:20 — fear of God before you; Psa 119:11 — word stored in heart) prescribes perceptive-enhancement measures. The implication: strengthening inner perception (of God's presence, of the act's moral quality) is the primary mechanism against wilful sinning — confirming that sinning involves a failure or suppression of that perception.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The perceptive pattern (primarily from 2Pe 2:14) reveals that sustained enticement distorts the perceptive faculty at its most basic level: the eyes become instruments of desire rather than neutral observation. When the heart has been "trained in greed," the perceptive faculty is recruited into the service of that training — it sees what greed seeks, not what is there. The perceptive corruption is thus both a symptom of the heart's training and a reinforcer of it: distorted perception feeds the distorted desire.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that the universal sin-condition is partly constituted by a perceptive blindness to itself: the condition hides its own nature from the person under it (Heb 3:13 — deceitfulness; Joh 9:41 — false certainty of seeing). This is why the characteristic requires external divine agency (Spirit's conviction — Joh 16:8; Jesus's coming and speaking — Joh 15:22; gospel proclamation — Act 13:38) to make the condition known. The condition generates the perceptive impairment that prevents its own recognition — a self-concealing feature that makes it both universal and universally unrecognised without divine intervention.

**[CHAR-12]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that sin's enslaving power is self-concealing: the enslaved person does not perceive themselves as enslaved (Joh 8:33 — claiming never to have been enslaved while Jesus declares their slavery). This perceptive impairment is what makes the enslaving power's grip so effective: the person cannot escape what they do not perceive as captivity. It also explains why the liberation-declaration must come from outside (Jesus's word — Joh 8:34; apostolic declaration — 1Jo 3:8/9) rather than from the enslaved person's own perceptive recognition.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that the divine record operates partly through perceptive concealment: the record exists before God regardless of whether the person perceives it, but the person's perceptive engagement with it is variable and distortable. Jer 16:10 (incomprehension under judgment), Hos 12:8 (prosperity-induced blindness), and Isa 3:9 (sin publicly displayed without shame) represent the full perceptive failure spectrum — from genuine incomprehension to wealth-induced blindness to conscience-deadened display. The perceptive faculty's restoration is the first step toward the record being addressed (Lev 4:23 — "made known to him" → brings offering).

**[CHAR-14]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that the characteristic requires perceptive engagement at both ends: recognition of sin (Lev 4:14 — perceiving the committed sin) enables seeking, and recognition of forgiveness magnitude (Luk 7:47 — perceiving how much has been forgiven) deepens the response. The characteristic thus both depends on and deepens the perceptive faculty: impaired perception (unrecognised sin — no seeking initiated) blocks the characteristic; restored perception (forgiveness received and its magnitude perceived) deepens love.

**[CHAR-15]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that the generational sin-pattern creates a *perceptive insulation* against divine evidence: Psa 78:32 — wonders witnessed but not believed — the inherited unbelief filters out the faith-producing implications of divine acts. This perceptive insulation is one of the mechanisms that makes generational sin self-perpetuating: the community cannot easily break the pattern because even direct divine intervention (wonders) does not penetrate the perceptive barrier created by the inherited unbelief orientation.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that the sinner-identity creates two characteristic perceptive distortions: (1) the sinner's impaired self-perception (Amo 9:10 — seeing no danger; extreme-type sinners not recognising their condition); and (2) the observer's impaired perception of others (Joh 9:24 — wrongly labelling Jesus a sinner; Luk 7:39 — perceiving the woman's sinner-label as contagion). The corrective perceptive acts — Luk 5:8 (accurate self-perception), Luk 13:2 (Jesus correcting misperception), Joh 9:25 (refusing the false verdict) — are the exceptions that mark the impairment as the norm.

**[CHAR-17]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that the guilt-state operates in both directions on perception: it can sharpen retrospective moral perception (Gen 42:21 — seeing past cruelty clearly under guilt's pressure) and distort present-moment God-perception (Eze 9:9 — misreading God as absent). The productive use of the perceptive faculty under guilt is retrospective (perceiving what was done); the distortion is prospective (misperceiving God's response to the guilt).

**[CHAR-18]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals an inverse relationship between the depth of iniquity's entrenchment and the accuracy of the person's self-perception: the more entrenched the iniquity (Psa 36:2 — the hardened wicked; Hos 12:8 — self-deceived Ephraim), the less accurately the person perceives it. The corrective is always from God's side: Job 13:23 — divine disclosure; Jer 14:7 — "our iniquities testify against us" — the iniquity itself becoming the witness that overrides false perception. God's perfect perception (Jer 16:17 — omniscient gaze) stands against the human's distorted self-perception.

**[CHAR-19]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that transgression progressively impairs self-perception of the transgression itself: the further transgression is entrenched, the less the person perceives it (Isa 58:1 — needs prophetic declaration; Isa 46:8 — must be told to recall). The corrective always requires external input: God's declaration (Isa 58:1), prophetic courage (Mic 3:8 — "I am filled with power... to declare to Jacob his transgression"), or divine illumination (Job 13:23). God's perception of transgression (Amos 5:12 — "I know how many") never diminishes and stands against the human's progressively impaired self-perception.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The pattern reveals that CHAR-2 is constituted precisely by a perceptive gap — the space between available sensory/cognitive input and what would be needed to prevent the inadvertent violation. This is what makes unintentional sinning categorically different from wilful sinning (where perception registers the wrong and the will overrides it) and from conscience suppression (where perception registers but is refused). The perceptive gap is the defining inner-being structure of the characteristic: close the gap (provide the missing information) and the characteristic resolves — either the person does not sin in the first place (knowing the prohibition) or the sin transitions to the confession-and-remedy phase once disclosed.

**[CHAR-20]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that faithlessness systematically impairs the self-perception needed for recognition and repentance (2Ch 28:22 — Ahaz doesn't see faithlessness causing distress) while leaving intact the perception of others' faithlessness (Jer 12:6 — the prophet perceiving family members' treachery; Hab 1:13 — the prophet perceiving traitors swallowing the righteous). The perceptive asymmetry is characteristic of CHAR-20: the faithless person sees others' treachery but not their own; the covenant-faithful person sees faithlessness clearly in both directions.

**[CHAR-21]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that perversion's most damaging inner effect is the blinding of the cognitive-perceptive faculty. Exo 23:8 and Deu 16:19's "blinds the eyes" is the corpus's most explicit perceptive-faculty statement: the perversion of judgment through bribery does not merely distort what is seen but removes the capacity to see clearly. 1Ti 6:5 — "deprived of the truth" — the final state of mind-depravity is blindness to truth itself. The perceptive pattern confirms: perversion does not merely colour what is perceived but eliminates the perceptive capacity at the relevant moral and theological levels.

**[CHAR-22]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that Zep 3:5's "the unjust knows no shame" is CHAR-22's most diagnostically significant inner-being statement: the absence of shame-perception is the marker of fully constituted injustice. The perceptive trajectory runs: God-perception diminished (Psa 53:1 — heart-atheism) → moral shame-perception eliminated (Zep 3:5). The restoration path requires the inverse: God-fear reactivated (2Ch 19:7 — "let the fear of the Lord be upon you") restoring the moral perceptive faculty.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that confession is the *externalisation of moral perception*: what the perceptive faculty has seen about the sin, the confession names aloud. The quality of the confession (precise vs formulaic, extended vs brief) thus reflects the quality of the moral perception that produced it. Dan 9:5's multi-dimensional confession reflects high-resolution moral perception; Exo 9:27's "this time I have sinned" reflects minimal perception — enough to produce the formula, not enough to drive sustained moral engagement with what was done.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that conscience suppression is fundamentally *a failure of inner moral sight*: the characteristic defines a person whose inner senses cannot accurately perceive their own moral condition. This is why external correction is required — Jer 2:35 (divine judgment announced), Jer 16:10 (prophetic word delivered), 1Cor 15:34 (apostolic rebuke) — because the internal perceptive faculty has failed and must be replaced by external moral input. The characteristic reveals that accurate moral self-perception is a faculty that requires maintenance through the fear of God (Ecc 8:12) and knowledge of God (1Cor 15:34).

**[CHAR-5]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that refusal to repent is sustained partly through a *perceptive distortion of moral gravity*: the sinful course is perceived as lighter than it is (1Ki 16:31) or as normal by habituation (the Kings pattern). Correcting refusal to repent therefore requires not only volitional change but perceptive re-calibration — the person must come to perceive the sin's gravity accurately before the will is sufficiently motivated to turn. Neh 9:29's warnings were an attempt to re-calibrate perceptive assessment from outside; their failure shows that external warning alone cannot correct the perceptive distortion when the will is entrenched.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that habitual defection and spiritual perception are structurally incompatible: 1Jo 3:6's "never seen him" confirms that sustained habitual sinning correlates with a fundamental perceptive blindness to God. The characteristic is not merely a behavioural pattern but a perceptive-epistemic condition: the one who keeps on sinning cannot see God. Correcting habitual defection therefore requires not only behavioural change but a restoration of perceptive capacity — the ability to see and know Christ that abiding in him provides (1Jo 3:6 — the abiding relationship as the condition under which sinning does not dominate).

**[CHAR-7]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that contagious sin exploits the community's designed capacity to trust authority: the authority relationship is a perceptive short-cut — the community accepts what the leader presents without full independent moral assessment, because authority is designed to be trusted. Contagious sin operates through this perceptive short-cut, transmitting the sinning direction through the very channel that the image-bearing authority relationship was designed to use for moral formation toward God. Correcting contagious sin's perceptive bypass requires the community to develop independent moral assessment of their leader's direction against God's standard — which is exactly what prophetic confrontation (1Ki 16:2 — God's word through the prophet charging the king) is designed to provide.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that political revolt requires and exercises the perceptive faculty in the political-strategic domain: reading the governing authority's vulnerability, assessing the timing, and identifying the moment when revolt is viable. This is not moral perception (seeing one's own sin) but political perception (seeing the opportunity for successful revolt). The corpus's political-register focus means the perceptive faculty is engaged in the strategic-political domain rather than the moral-spiritual domain.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that sinful speech is both a symptom and a deepener of perceptive impairment: the corrupted heart produces speech that further distorts the speaker's perception of reality. The scribes' misidentification of Jesus as a blasphemer (VCG-02) shows the endpoint of perceptive distortion — when sinful speech becomes the lens through which divine reality is misread, the person cannot perceive the truth even when it is standing before them. The characteristic thus impairs perception in a self-reinforcing loop: impaired perception enables sinful speech; sinful speech deepens the impairment.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The consistent perceptive impairment reveals that wickedness-as-settled-person-identity involves a systematic closure of the inner faculty through which God and moral reality are apprehended. This is not accidental — it is the functional consequence of the practical atheism at the characteristic's core (VCG-02: Psa 10:4). The person who excludes God from their thought-life (Psa 10:4) necessarily loses the capacity to perceive the divine perspective on their situation (Isa 26:10). The perceptive pattern reveals that wickedness is self-reinforcing through this perceptual closure: the less the wicked person can perceive moral reality, the more deeply settled the characteristic becomes. This is a diagnostic finding about the characteristic's internal dynamics.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The perceptive engagement pattern reveals that evil as constitutional inner nature has corrupted the person's evaluative and orientational perception — they see, but are constitutionally inclined to evaluate what they see according to a darkened standard. Mat 6:23 (VCG-03) reveals the constitutive link: the eye's badness is not merely a failure of individual perceptions but a constitutional state of the perceptive faculty that determines what the whole person apprehends. This reveals the characteristic as a condition that has compromised the primary incoming-orientation faculty — before the person acts, before they speak, the perceptive faculty through which they receive and assess reality is already constitutionally corrupted.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The dual pattern — impaired perception in the abominable, heightened perception in the grieving — reveals that the characteristic's relationship to moral perception is a diagnostic indicator of the conscience's state. Isa 44:19 (vc=65961 — VCG-05) identifies the absence of discernment as what enables abomination without self-recognition. Eze 9:4 (vc=1698 — VCG-04) shows that the capacity to perceive abomination in others is the mark of a functioning moral-perceptive conscience. The pattern reveals the characteristic as one that progressively closes moral perception in the person who practises abomination, while it sharpens moral perception in those whose conscience remains functional and responsive.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals a distinctive feature of idolatrous abomination: the characteristic operates through the visual-desire appetite more than other M10b characteristics. The idolatrous object is presented as visually attractive — Eze 7:20 (vc=65909 — VCG-05): "his beautiful ornament" converted into idols — the beauty of the material is what draws. This visual-attractiveness mechanism explains the Deuteronomic emphasis on destroying the idol-objects (Deu 7:25 — VCG-02: "burn with fire") and not coveting what is on them — the perceptive-desire faculty is the primary entry-point for the characteristic. The perceptive pattern reveals CHAR-4 as operating through visual desire in a way that distinguishes it from CHAR-1 (which operates through inner voice) and CHAR-2 (which operates through the heart's treasury).

**[CHAR-5]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals that iniquity as scheming specifically requires a particular perceptive orientation — the "watching to do evil" (Isa 29:20 — VCG-02) and listening to wicked lips (Pro 17:4 — VCG-03) show the characteristic as actively deploying the perceptive faculties in the service of harm-generation. The concomitant moral-knowledge blindness (Psa 14:4 — VCG-03) is not accidental but functionally linked: the inner sight directed toward opportunities for evil cannot simultaneously attend to moral reality. The perceptive pattern reveals the characteristic as perceptively focussed and functionally selective — able to spot opportunities for harm while blind to moral truth.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals a distinctive split in the characteristic: the physical perceptive faculty is intact (pain and judgment are felt — Rev 16:9/11/21 — VCG-01) while the moral-spiritual perceptive faculty has failed (Jude 10 — VCG-01: not understanding). This split confirms that the characteristic is primarily a will-phenomenon, not a perception-phenomenon: the hardened will can perceive the divine power behind the judgment (Rev 16:9: "who had power over these plagues") yet refuse to respond rightly to what it perceives. The perceptive pattern reveals the characteristic as a post-perceptual failure — not a failure to see but a refusal to respond rightly to what is seen.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's perceptive pattern reveals that moral-spiritual blindness is a defining characteristic of M10b evil-conditions — not incidental but structural. The person constituted by M10b characteristics cannot accurately perceive the moral reality of their own condition. This perceptive failure is documented across all six characteristics and explains why external prophetic confrontation (naming abominations — Eze 16:2; Char 4 reformers removing idols — VCG-03; divine instruction opening the ear — Job 36:10) is necessary: the person's own perceptive faculty cannot generate the corrective data that would initiate departure from the characteristic.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The pervasive engagement with visual assessment (the leprous-disease priestly examination in Lev 13-14, M10c-B-VCG-02) reveals that the characteristic treats the bodily surface as a readable text — the skin's appearance encodes the person's sacral status. Simultaneously, the VCG-01 evidence (defilement hidden from perception) reveals that the characteristic is not reducible to what the person perceives: the condition exists objectively prior to awareness. This shows the characteristic as operating in a domain that partially exceeds the perceptive faculty's reach, requiring conscience to supplement perception.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The perceptive engagement reveals the characteristic as self-obscuring at the advanced stage: the condition suppresses the perceptive faculty that would recognise it. The person fully in the moral-inner defilement-state can no longer perceive it as defilement (Eph 4:19 — callousness; Tit 1:15 reference — nothing pure to the defiled). The characteristic is thus not simply a condition alongside normal inner functioning but one that compromises the inner faculties' ability to perceive themselves correctly. This distinguishes it from Characteristic 1 (Ritual defilement-state), which the person can recognise through the categorical system; Characteristic 2 corrupts the very instrument of recognition.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals the characteristic as self-obscuring in the present and self-revealing in the eschatological future. The community in the defilement-state cannot perceive its own condition (Jer 2:23), while God perceives it clearly (Eze 23:13, Hos 5:3) and prophetic speech confronts the gap. The future restoration is precisely the moment when the community's perception will align with God's — they will see what God has always seen (Eze 20:43). This reveals the characteristic as involving an epistemological disruption: the defiled community cannot assess itself correctly, requiring divine and prophetic counter-testimony.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The perceptive pattern reveals the characteristic as selectively targeting the person's relational perceptive faculties (hearing and speech), precisely the faculties required for relationship with God and with others. The selective suppression of hearing and speech reveals the characteristic as operating to isolate the person relationally — cutting off their perceptive access to the voices of God and neighbour. This is consistent with the broader pattern of communal severance (Mar 5:2).

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's perceptive engagement pattern reveals a consistent structural feature: defilement correlates with perceptive distortion at the self-assessment level. Across all four characteristics, the person or community in the defilement-state faces a perceptive challenge in relation to their own condition. Characteristic 1: the condition can be incurred before perception catches it (Lev 5:2-3 — defilement hidden from the person). Characteristic 2: the advanced condition corrupts the very faculty that should perceive it (Tit 1:15 reference — nothing pure to the defiled). Characteristic 3: the community actively denies its own condition (Jer 2:23 — "I am not unclean"). Characteristic 4: the person cannot perceive or articulate their own condition from within the domination. The cluster's perceptive deficit is universal: in every register of defilement, the defiled person has a compromised capacity to accurately perceive their own defiled state. This is one of the cluster's most important findings for Session C: defilement impairs the very perceptive faculty that would recognise it — confirming that external intervention (priestly examination, prophetic confrontation, divine command) is always required to make the condition visible.

The perceptive engagement pattern reveals that forgiveness is **not primarily perceptive in its operation** — it does not primarily function through the inner senses — but the **conditions of its reception and blockage** involve perception centrally. The person who cannot perceive the source and depth of forgiveness available cannot receive it. The person who has received it deeply demonstrates an enhanced perceptive orientation.

This suggests forgiveness operates **downstream of perception**: correct spiritual discernment is a precondition for genuine reception; received forgiveness then reorganises and deepens the perceptive capacity. It does not function as a sense or perception itself but it requires perception as an access-condition and generates enhanced perception as a downstream effect.

Grace is inherently perceptual in its operation — it requires the inner person to see, hear, and recognise what is being given. Grace that is not perceived is grace that does not land (SD043: acharistos). The perceptive faculty is integral, not incidental: grace requires recognition to complete its operation. This is why impaired perception simultaneously blocks reception — and why grace itself must first enable perception before it can be received.

*New finding as a T3-level statement: the integral relationship between grace and perception — requiring perception to complete its operation, and enabling that perception — is not previously stated in these terms.*

The consistent sight-trigger pattern reveals that compassion is fundamentally a responsive characteristic — it does not arise in the absence of perceived need. This distinguishes it from characteristics that operate independently of external stimulus (e.g., integrity, which operates whether or not one is observed; faithfulness, which is constitutive regardless of circumstances). Compassion requires the other to be present and perceptible.

This has a structural implication: compassion's operation is contingent on perception, but its character is not contingent on the perceived person's merit. The splanchnizō movements in the Gospels are not triggered by the moral worthiness of the recipients — they are triggered by the sight of suffering, need, and lostness. Jon 4:11 (God's pity for Nineveh) is triggered by the sight of people "who do not know their right hand from their left" — moral ignorance, not moral achievement. Compassion is perceptively triggered but merit-independent in its response.

The non-engagement pattern (the priest and Levite in Luke 10, the judicial eye that will not pity) reveals the complementary truth: the suppression of compassion requires a deliberate act of non-seeing — a refusal to let the perception of need produce its natural response. Compassion's connection to sight is so strong that suppressing it requires overriding what the eye generates.

The pattern reveals that contrition is constitutively open rather than closed in its perceptive orientation. The contrite inner being is oriented outward — toward God's word, toward what God will give (joy, gladness) — rather than inward in a self-referential way. This is significant: contrition could be a purely inward condition of self-preoccupation, but the verse evidence consistently presents it as oriented toward God and toward what will come from God. The contrite person is perceptively open and expectant. This perceptive openness distinguishes contrition from guilt-paralysis (a possible alternative — being so turned inward on one's failure that the perceptive faculty is closed).

The pattern reveals that fellowship operates partly *through* the perceptive faculty as a channel: proclamation enters through hearing to create fellowship (1Jo 1:3); wounding reaches through somatic sensation to inner purification (Pro 20:30); seeing what God has done creates the testimony that extends fellowship (1Jo 1:3). Fellowship is not primarily a cognitive or emotive phenomenon — it is first encountered perceptively (hearing, seeing, experiencing). This perceptive character is consistent with the Hebrew vocabulary's emphasis on joining and binding, which are contact-based physical images.

The perceptive engagement of goodness reveals that it is not primarily an abstract ethical category but an experiential reality that must be encountered and tasted. Goodness is known through contact, not inference. This is structurally consistent with the Hebrew tov's phenomenological root (what is genuinely pleasant, beneficial, and right — experienced as such). The pattern reveals that goodness has an inherently perceptual character — it calls for encounter, not merely assent. The Haman diagnostic (Est 5:9) confirms this: he experienced a surface perception of well-being without genuine perceptual encounter with goodness as rooted in God. Perception without genuine encounter produces the counterfeit. The nature of goodness is therefore inherently experiential and perceptually demanding. (OBS-067-OBS-025, OBS-067-OBS-041, SBF-067-Q088)

The pattern reveals that love functions as a perceptual lens — it determines what the inner person sees as real and significant. Rightly directed love opens perception to what is true and lovely; misdirected love closes perception to correction and light. This means love is not merely affective but epistemic: it shapes the person's capacity to perceive. This is consistent with the epistemic finding in Q&A-153 (L-012): love constitutes the relational structure within which knowing becomes possible. The pattern also reveals that love's perceptual function is asymmetric — righteous love opens perception outward (toward God, the beloved, the truth); disordered love closes perception inward (toward the self and its preferred objects). Love and perception are constitutively linked: you see what you love.

Mercy's face-and-seeing engagement reveals that mercy is relational perception realised — it is not anonymous compassion but face-to-face recognition of the person. The mercy-seeking cry is directed toward a person (Jesus, Son of David — Mar 10:48, OBS-111-054); the mercy received is the restoration of sight (physical seeing restored by the one whose face mercy-seekers cry toward). The perceptive faculty is therefore both the medium through which mercy is sought (seeing the merciful face) and the gift mercy restores (sight given to the blind). OBS-111-054, OBS-111-040.

The pattern reveals contrition as a perceptive-opening event — the inner breaking simultaneously opens the person to divine address. The hardened heart is perceptively closed; the contrite heart is perceptively receptive. Contrition is the condition in which the perceptive faculty is most available to God's word and God's presence. OBS-030-028, OBS-030-060, OBS-030-062.

The pattern reveals perception as a prerequisite for rightly directed fellowship and a casualty of misdirected fellowship. The person who fellowships well must first perceive well; the person whose fellowship is misdirected is progressively less able to perceive the error. OBS-062-042, OBS-062-049.

The pattern: perception of forgiveness's magnitude determines the love-response. Shallow perception → shallow love. Deep perception → deep love. Forgiveness both requires and deepens perception of divine character. The perceptive faculty is both the gate to receiving forgiveness and the beneficiary of having received it. OBS-064-029.

The pattern reveals that covenant is not a self-activating inner-being reality — it depends on an open perceptive faculty as its gateway. Covenant cannot be received by the person who will not hear; it cannot transform the person whose perceptive faculty is veiled or hardened. Conversely, the new covenant's promise is precisely to restore and enable perception: writing on the heart produces knowing (Jer 31:34), and knowing is a form of heightened inner perception of God. This means covenant and perception have a reciprocal relationship: open perception enables covenant reception; covenant transformation deepens and enlarges perception. The pattern shows that covenant is the structured framework within which the inner perceptive faculty either opens toward God (covenant faithfulness) or closes away from him (covenant breach and hardening).

The perception engagement reveals that peace is not only a passive condition (a state received) but an enabling posture — the person at peace is constitutionally equipped to perceive things they cannot hear when restless. The demamah threshold (1Ki 19:12) is analytically significant: the divine voice comes not in wind, earthquake, or fire (the dramatic) but in the still small voice — and only the person who has moved through silence can hear it. This means peace has a gnomic/perceptual consequence: the peace-bearing person perceives differently. Peace as the enabling condition for divine perception is a new finding.

The pattern reveals that this characteristic has a relational-perceptive architecture: inner-being giving is grounded in prior perception (God hears suffering before giving; Spirit-endowment enables the human to hear instruction) and it shapes subsequent perception (failure to give glory produces perceptive darkening; receiving eschatological giving restores responsiveness — Hos 2:15, OBS-060-050). The characteristic is not perception itself, but it operates through perception as both its precondition and its consequence. This reveals that inner-being giving is not blind action — it is responsive, attentive, and formative of the recipient's perceptive capacity.
